# Cleaning and Recoding {#sec-cleaning}

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("_common.R")
brfss <- readRDS(file.path(processed_dir, "01-brfss.rds"))
```

Raw BRFSS answers are numeric codes. Cleaning turns them into labeled categories that R and
readers understand. It is also where most analysis errors start: a code that slips through
unrecoded (a 99 for "refused" read as an income group) or a missing value silently turned into
"no" changes every result that follows.

This chapter follows four rules:

1. **Declare first.** Before using an item, write down every value the codebook allows.
2. **Check.** Stop if the data hold any other value.
3. **Recode explicitly.** Map every value, including missing ones, by hand; never rely on a
   default to absorb something unexpected.
4. **Count.** Report how many answers each coding rule changes (@sec-decisions).

## Step 1: Declare what each item can be

The values below come from the
[BRFSS 2024 codebook](https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/annual_data/annual_2024.html). BRFSS uses
the same codes for non-answers throughout: 7 (or 77) for "Don't know/Not sure", 9 (or 99) for
"Refused", and a blank (`NA` in R) for "Not asked or missing".

```{r}
#| label: declare
# Possible values of each item in the BRFSS 2024 codebook. Blank (NA) means "not asked or
# missing".
item_values <- list(
  DIABETE4 = c(1:4, 7, 9), # 1 Yes; 2 Yes, but only during pregnancy; 3 No;
  # 4 No, prediabetes or borderline; 7 Don't know; 9 Refused
  GENHLTH = c(1:5, 7, 9), # 1 Excellent; 2 Very good; 3 Good; 4 Fair; 5 Poor;
  # 7 Don't know; 9 Refused
  MEDCOST1 = c(1, 2, 7, 9), # 1 Yes; 2 No; 7 Don't know; 9 Refused
  INCOME3 = c(1:11, 77, 99), # 1 Less than $10,000 ... 11 $200,000 or more;
  # 77 Don't know; 99 Refused
  `_AGE_G` = 1:6, # 1 18-24; 2 25-34; 3 35-44; 4 45-54; 5 55-64; 6 65+
  `_AGE80` = 18:80, # CDC-imputed age in years; 80 means 80 or older
  SEXVAR = 1:2, # 1 Male; 2 Female
  `_IMPRACE` = 1:6, # 1 White; 2 Black; 3 Asian; 4 American Indian or Alaska
  # Native (all non-Hispanic); 5 Hispanic; 6 Other, non-Hispanic
  EDUCA = c(1:6, 9), # 1 Never attended ... 6 College 4 years or more; 9 Refused
  EMPLOY1 = 1:9, # 1 Employed for wages ... 8 Unable to work; 9 Refused
  `_STATE` = c(1, 2, 4:6, 8:13, 15:42, 44:46, 48:51, 53:56, 66, 72, 78) # FIPS codes
)
# The design variables and the CDC-imputed items are never blank.
never_blank <- c(
  "_LLCPWT",
  "_STSTR",
  "_PSU",
  "_STATE",
  "_AGE_G",
  "_AGE80",
  "SEXVAR",
  "_IMPRACE"
)
```

The 53 state codes are the 2024 codebook's: the 50 states except Tennessee (47), plus the
District of Columbia (11), Guam (66), Puerto Rico (72), and the US Virgin Islands (78).

## Step 2: Check the data against the codebook

A codebook can be wrong, and a file can change between releases. This check compares every
observed value with the declaration and stops, naming each item and value, if anything else
appears. It is silent when the data are as declared.

```{r}
#| label: check-values
# Check: every value is in the codebook.
unexpected <- purrr::imap(item_values, \(values, item) {
  setdiff(brfss[[item]], c(values, NA))
}) |>
  purrr::compact()
if (length(unexpected) > 0) {
  stop(
    "Values not in the codebook: ",
    paste0(
      names(unexpected),
      " (",
      purrr::map_chr(unexpected, toString),
      ")",
      collapse = "; "
    )
  )
}
# Check: no blanks where the codebook has none, and every weight is positive.
stopifnot(!anyNA(brfss[never_blank]), all(brfss[["_LLCPWT"]] > 0))
```

Here is one item's raw distribution, before recoding:

```{r}
#| label: raw-income
tidylog::count(brfss, INCOME3)
```

## Step 3: Recode

`dplyr::recode_values()` maps each code (left of `~`) to a value (right of `~`). With
`unmatched = "error"`, any code we did not list stops the run, so nothing can slip through.
`tidylog::mutate()` works like `dplyr::mutate()` but reports what each new variable looks like,
including its share of missing values.

Four decisions are built into this recoding (@sec-decisions lists them with counts):

- **Non-answers become missing.** "Don't know", "refused", and blank tell us nothing about a
  person's true value, so they become `NA`. @sec-imputation fills them in by multiple
  imputation rather than dropping those people.
- **Values that other answers settle are coded, not left missing.** A woman told she had
  diabetes *only during pregnancy* (`DIABETE4 = 2`) does not have diabetes now, so she is
  coded "No".
- **Age and race and ethnicity come from CDC's imputed versions.** CDC fills the few missing
  answers for these weighting variables (`_AGE_G`, `_IMPRACE`), so they are never blank.
  Six age groups adjust for age much better than two.
- **Reference groups come first.** The first level of each factor is the comparison group in
  the models: the lowest income group, ages 18-24, female, and non-Hispanic White (the
  largest group).

```{r}
#| label: recode
brfss_clean <- brfss |>
  tidylog::mutate(
    diabetes = dplyr::recode_values(
      DIABETE4,
      1 ~ "Yes",
      c(2, 3) ~ "No", # 2 = told only during pregnancy: no diabetes now
      4 ~ "Prediabetes",
      c(7, 9, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("No", "Prediabetes", "Yes")),
    genhlth = dplyr::recode_values(
      GENHLTH,
      1 ~ "Excellent",
      2 ~ "Very good",
      3 ~ "Good",
      4 ~ "Fair",
      5 ~ "Poor",
      c(7, 9, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("Excellent", "Very good", "Good", "Fair", "Poor")),
    cost_barrier = dplyr::recode_values(
      MEDCOST1,
      1 ~ "Yes",
      2 ~ "No",
      c(7, 9, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    income = dplyr::recode_values(
      INCOME3,
      1:4 ~ "Less than $25,000",
      5:6 ~ "$25,000 to $49,999",
      7:8 ~ "$50,000 to $99,999",
      9:11 ~ "$100,000 or more",
      c(77, 99, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(
        levels = c(
          "Less than $25,000",
          "$25,000 to $49,999",
          "$50,000 to $99,999",
          "$100,000 or more"
        )
      ),
    age_group = dplyr::recode_values(
      `_AGE_G`,
      1 ~ "18-24",
      2 ~ "25-34",
      3 ~ "35-44",
      4 ~ "45-54",
      5 ~ "55-64",
      6 ~ "65 or older",
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(
        levels = c("18-24", "25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64", "65 or older")
      ),
    age = as.numeric(`_AGE80`),
    sex = dplyr::recode_values(
      SEXVAR,
      1 ~ "Male",
      2 ~ "Female",
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("Female", "Male")),
    race_eth = dplyr::recode_values(
      `_IMPRACE`,
      1 ~ "Non-Hispanic White",
      2 ~ "Non-Hispanic Black",
      3 ~ "Non-Hispanic Asian",
      4 ~ "Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native",
      5 ~ "Hispanic",
      6 ~ "Non-Hispanic other race",
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(
        levels = c(
          "Non-Hispanic White",
          "Non-Hispanic Black",
          "Non-Hispanic Asian",
          "Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native",
          "Hispanic",
          "Non-Hispanic other race"
        )
      ),
    education = dplyr::recode_values(
      EDUCA,
      1:3 ~ "Less than high school",
      4 ~ "High school graduate",
      5 ~ "Some college",
      6 ~ "College graduate",
      c(9, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(
        levels = c(
          "Less than high school",
          "High school graduate",
          "Some college",
          "College graduate"
        )
      ),
    employment = dplyr::recode_values(
      EMPLOY1,
      1:2 ~ "Employed",
      3:4 ~ "Out of work",
      5:6 ~ "Homemaker or student",
      7 ~ "Retired",
      8 ~ "Unable to work",
      c(9, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(
        levels = c(
          "Employed",
          "Out of work",
          "Homemaker or student",
          "Retired",
          "Unable to work"
        )
      ),
    state = factor(`_STATE`),
    # 0/1 outcomes for the models. `==` keeps missing values missing (`%in%` would not).
    diabetes_yes = as.integer(diabetes == "Yes"),
    fair_poor = as.integer(genhlth == "Fair" | genhlth == "Poor")
  ) |>
  # PSU codes repeat across strata: number each stratum-PSU pair.
  tidylog::mutate(psu_id = dplyr::cur_group_id(), .by = c(`_STSTR`, `_PSU`))
```

::: callout-warning
## A common trap with missing values

`genhlth %in% c("Fair", "Poor")` returns `FALSE` (not `NA`) when `genhlth` is missing, so
everyone with a missing answer would be counted as being in good health. Comparisons with
`==` keep missing values missing.
:::

::: callout-note
## Why a new PSU identifier?

In BRFSS, PSU codes are only unique *within* a stratum: PSU 1 in one stratum is a different
phone number from PSU 1 in another. `survey::svydesign()` can combine them itself
(`nest = TRUE`). Numbering each stratum-PSU pair once gives globally unique integer IDs and
avoids repeated relabeling and a large nesting cross-tabulation. The speed difference
depends on the installed survey backend; the weights, strata and clusters are unchanged. There are
`r format(dplyr::n_distinct(brfss_clean$psu_id), big.mark = ",")` pairs for
`r format(nrow(brfss_clean), big.mark = ",")` respondents: in BRFSS each respondent is their
own PSU.
:::

## Step 4: Check the recoding

The `unmatched = "error"` arguments already guarantee that every code was mapped. Four more
checks confirm the rules we rely on later, including that every PSU identifier sits in a
single stratum, which lets the survey designs in later chapters skip their own (slow) check
of the same thing.

```{r}
#| label: check-recode
# Check: the "only during pregnancy" answers are now "No", and the 0/1 outcomes are
# missing exactly where the outcomes are.
stopifnot(
  all(brfss_clean$diabetes[brfss_clean$DIABETE4 %in% 2] == "No"),
  identical(is.na(brfss_clean$diabetes_yes), is.na(brfss_clean$diabetes)),
  identical(is.na(brfss_clean$fair_poor), is.na(brfss_clean$genhlth))
)
# Check: each PSU identifier belongs to exactly one stratum (PSUs are nested in strata).
stopifnot(
  nrow(dplyr::distinct(brfss_clean, psu_id, `_STSTR`)) ==
    dplyr::n_distinct(brfss_clean$psu_id)
)
```

A crosswalk lists every raw code next to the value it became, with the number of
respondents. It is the record of the recoding, and @sec-decisions shows it in full. Here is
income:

```{r}
#| label: crosswalk
recoded <- c(
  DIABETE4 = "diabetes",
  GENHLTH = "genhlth",
  MEDCOST1 = "cost_barrier",
  INCOME3 = "income",
  `_AGE_G` = "age_group",
  `_AGE80` = "age",
  SEXVAR = "sex",
  `_IMPRACE` = "race_eth",
  EDUCA = "education",
  EMPLOY1 = "employment"
)
crosswalk <- purrr::imap(recoded, \(new, item) {
  return(dplyr::count(
    brfss_clean,
    code = as.numeric(.data[[item]]),
    value = as.character(.data[[new]])
  ))
}) |>
  purrr::list_rbind(names_to = "item")
dplyr::filter(crosswalk, item == "INCOME3")
```

Income is missing for
`r format(sum(is.na(brfss_clean$income)), big.mark = ",")` respondents
(`r round(100 * mean(is.na(brfss_clean$income)), 1)`%): more than any other variable in this
book. @sec-descriptives looks at who they are.

## Step 5: Keep the analysis variables and save

`tidylog::select()` keeps the recoded variables, renames the design variables so they no
longer need backticks, and drops the raw codes.

```{r}
#| label: save
brfss_clean <- brfss_clean |>
  tidylog::select(
    weight = `_LLCPWT`,
    strata = `_STSTR`,
    psu_id,
    state, # survey design
    diabetes,
    diabetes_yes,
    genhlth,
    fair_poor,
    cost_barrier, # outcomes
    income, # exposure
    age_group,
    age, # numeric age for the descriptive example; models use age_group
    sex,
    race_eth, # covariates
    education,
    employment # auxiliary variables
  )
dplyr::glimpse(brfss_clean)

saveRDS(brfss_clean, file.path(processed_dir, "02-brfss-clean.rds"))
saveRDS(crosswalk, file.path(processed_dir, "02-crosswalk.rds"))
```
